## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- **Build** a content-based recommender from item features (genre vectors + cosine), **compute** a content profile by hand on L22's toy, and **explain** its tied scores and over-specialization. *(Apply)*
- **Distinguish** content-based, demographic, and knowledge-based filtering by the information each needs, **map** each to the cold-start gap it closes, and **recognize** that being able to run on a new user is not the same as predicting better. *(Understand / Analyze)*
- **Explain** hybrid recommenders (switching vs. weighted) and **build** a weighted blend of a content score and a collaborative score. *(Understand / Apply)*
- **Evaluate** recommenders on a held-out split with **RMSE** and **MAE**, **read** the accuracy ladder by the size of each step, and **run** a new-user test. *(Apply / Analyze)*

## Why This Matters

L22 left two questions open. First, collaborative filtering is **blind to anyone new**: a brand-new
user has no ratings to find neighbors from, and a brand-new movie has no ratings to be a neighbor —
the **cold-start** problem. Second, the top-N lists *looked* reasonable, but looking reasonable is not
a measurement. This lesson supplies the rest of the recommender family — the approaches that work
without the target's rating history — and the discipline that tells you whether any recommender is
actually any good.

## Content-Based Filtering

Collaborative filtering ignored *what* an item is. **Content-based filtering** does the opposite: it
recommends items whose **features** match the ones you liked. MovieLens tags every movie with 19
**genre** flags, so each movie is a 0/1 vector in "genre space." Build a user's **content profile** by
adding up the genre vectors of the movies they rated, each weighted by how far that rating sat from
their own average — the genres they reliably like come out large and positive, the ones they dislike
go negative. Then score every unseen movie by the **cosine similarity** (L18) between its genre vector
and that profile.

### Ana again

Take L22's toy. Ana rated *Terminator* 5, *Top Gun* 4, *Toy Story* 1 and *Lion King* 2, so her
average is 3 and her **centered** ratings are $+2, +1, -2, -1$. Their real MovieLens genres:
*Terminator* is Action, Sci-Fi, Thriller; *Top Gun* is Action, Romance; *Toy Story* is Animation,
Children, Comedy; *Lion King* is Animation, Children, Musical. Weight each movie's genres by Ana's
centered rating and add:

| Genre | Action | Sci-Fi | Thriller | Romance | Musical | Comedy | Animation | Children |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| **Ana's profile** | +3 | +2 | +2 | +1 | -1 | -2 | -3 | -3 |

The negative entries are the point. Genre vectors are all 0s and 1s, so they sit in L18's **positive
corner**; centering the ratings — the same move that rescued similarity in L22 — is what lets the
profile point *away* from the genres Ana dislikes.

Now score the two movies she has not seen. *Speed* is Action, Romance, Thriller, so its dot product
with the profile is $3 + 1 + 2 = 6$, and

$$\cos(\text{Ana}, \textit{Speed}) = \frac{6}{\sqrt{41}\,\sqrt{3}} = +0.541$$

*Aladdin* (Animation, Children, Comedy, Musical) scores $-0.703$. That is the verdict L22's
collaborative filtering reached — an action fan should see the action movie — but this time **no other
user was consulted**. And here is what collaborative filtering cannot do: add *Die Hard* (Action,
Thriller) to the catalog today, before anyone has rated it. There is no rating column to compare, so
collaborative filtering has nothing to say; content-based scores it at once, $+0.552$.

### A real user

![A horizontal bar chart of user 196's content profile across the 19 genres. Drama sticks out far to the right at about +5.2; Children, Fantasy, and Documentary are small and positive; Action at about -5.8, Adventure, Romance, Comedy, Sci-Fi, and War are negative. The chart shows one dominant liked genre and several disliked ones.](assets/l23_genre_profile.png)

User 196's profile is essentially one genre: Drama at +5.2, with Action (-5.8) and Adventure (-4.5)
pushed firmly away. The weakness, which you will see directly in the lab: **over-specialization**. A Drama lover gets a
list of nothing but Dramas; the method keeps serving the same flavor and rarely surprises you. Genres
are also a **coarse** feature: for user 196, 372 unseen movies are tagged only Drama, so all 372 share
one genre vector and tie at the same top score. The cosine cannot choose among them; the lab breaks
the tie with a stated **quality signal** (enough ratings, then the most-rated first). That quality
signal comes from ratings, so it is also what would hide a brand-new movie — Ana's *Die Hard* got a
score; a list filtered to well-rated movies could never show it.

## Demographic Filtering

**Demographic filtering** recommends by *who you are*. MovieLens ships real attributes in `u.user` —
age, gender, occupation — so you can ask "what do women aged 25-34 rate highest?" and recommend that
to a new member of that cohort. It needs **no ratings from the target user at all**, which is exactly
why it can greet a brand-new user the moment they sign up.

Being able to run is not the same as predicting well. In the lab you hold out a fifth of the users
entirely and predict their ratings two ways: by each movie's average over everyone (the **item mean**, the number behind L22's popularity list), and
by its average within the user's gender and age group. On MovieLens the two tie — the cohort adds
nothing that "how well-liked is this movie?" had not already captured. Demographics help only when
the attributes really predict taste. And grouping people by demographics raises fairness questions (a
theme for Unit VIII).

## Knowledge-Based Filtering

**Knowledge-based filtering** skips history entirely and works from **stated rules and constraints**.
A travel site that asks your dates, budget, and climate, then applies rules to filter the catalog, is
recommending without a single past rating. In the lab you build a tiny version: "a highly-rated Comedy
from the 1990s." Look at what that rule mixes. Genre and decade are **stated** constraints on the
movie's own attributes — known the day a movie is added. "Mean rating high enough, enough ratings to
trust" is a **quality filter borrowed from ratings**, and it cannot see a movie nobody has rated.
Knowledge-based systems in the wild mostly filter on item attributes (price, size, dates), which is why
they shine for **rare, high-stakes, or first-time** purchases — a house, a mortgage, a laptop — where
nobody has a rating history and the user can state what they need.

## Hybrid Recommenders

No single family wins everywhere, so real systems **combine** them — a **hybrid**:

- **Switching** — use one approach until another becomes possible: greet a new user with popular
  picks or a few questions, then **switch** to collaborative filtering once they have rated enough.
- **Weighted** — **blend** several scores into one (e.g. average a content score and a collaborative
  score), so each covers the other's blind spots. In the lab's blend for user 196, the content score
  decides *which shelf* (Drama) and matrix factorization orders the movies on it.

Every large platform ships a hybrid: it is the only way to be good for new users, new items, *and*
seasoned users at once.

## Cold Start, Resolved

Now L22's family table can be completed — the *fix* for each gap is "use a family that does not need
that history":

| Approach | Needs | New user | New item |
|----------|-------|----------|----------|
| **Collaborative filtering** | a ratings matrix | fails (no neighbors) | fails (no raters) |
| **Content-based** | item features | needs a few likes first | **works** (new item has features) |
| **Demographic** | user attributes | **runs** (no ratings needed) — predicts no better than the item mean here | not applicable |
| **Knowledge-based** | stated rules | **works** (asks directly) | **works** on stated constraints |
| **Hybrid** | a mix | depends on the mix: covers a gap if one of its parts does | same |

The standard playbook: start a new account with **popular** picks or a few questions, lean on
**content-based** for fresh items, and shift to **collaborative filtering** as real ratings accumulate.

## How to Evaluate a Recommender

A list that looks plausible can still be wrong. To *measure* a recommender, hide some of the known
ratings (a **train/test split**, exactly as in L14), predict them, and compare the predictions with the
truth using two standard error metrics:

$$\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n}\sum (\hat r - r)^2}, \qquad \text{MAE} = \tfrac{1}{n}\sum \lvert \hat r - r \rvert$$

**RMSE** (root mean squared error) squares each miss, so it punishes big misses hardest; **MAE** (mean
absolute error) is the plain average miss, in stars. Lower is better for both. (Predictions are
clipped to the 1-5 scale first, since no rating can fall outside it.) Run them on five rating
predictors — two plain averages, L22's baseline $\mu + b_u + b_i$, an item-item predictor built from L22's `S`, and L22's matrix
factorization — and an
**accuracy ladder** appears:

![A bar chart titled "The baseline does most of the work." Five bars of test RMSE, lower being better: global mean 1.124 and item mean 1.021 in light gray, the baseline mu + b_u + b_i 0.946 in dark gray, item-item collaborative filtering 0.945 in blue, and matrix factorization 0.922 in green. Between neighboring bars the steps are annotated: -0.103, -0.075, -0.001 marked as a tie, and -0.023.](assets/l23_rmse_ladder.png)

**Reading the output — by the size of each step:**

- **Knowing which movie** is the biggest step: from the global mean (1.124) to each movie's own
  average (1.021).
- **Knowing how generous this user is** comes next: L22's baseline $\mu + b_u + b_i$ reaches 0.946.
- **Item-item collaborative filtering** — L22's item similarity `S`, turned into a rating predictor
  with L22's user formula turned sideways — lands **level with the baseline** (0.945; on other random
  splits it comes out a hair above or below). On this data the neighbors add little that the two
  biases had not already captured.
- **Matrix factorization**, whose model *is* the baseline plus latent factors, takes the last real step,
  about 0.02, to **0.922**.

That is L22's finding again, now measured on ratings the models never saw: **the baseline does most of
the work, and the factors personalize at the margin.** The same kind of ladder — on Netflix's own
data — is what the Netflix Prize teams climbed, one small step at a time.

## Rating Error vs. Ranking Quality

One honest caveat. RMSE and MAE score how well you predict a *rating*, but what a user actually
experiences is the *ranking* — did the right items reach the top of the list? A model can shave RMSE
yet reorder the top 10 for the worse. Ranking is measured differently, with metrics like
**precision@k** (of the top k you showed, how many did the user like?). The ladder already hints at
the gap: L22 warned that the item-item weighted average floods a *top-N list* with movies only one
person rated, yet as a *rating predictor* it ties the baseline. We name precision@k here and the L24
project computes it; the key idea is that **predicting ratings well and ranking items well are related
but not the same goal.**

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Which approach is best?"** None alone — the right answer is almost always a **hybrid**. The
interesting question is not "which method" but "which method *for which situation*" (new user, new item,
rich history).

**"Isn't more data enough?"** More ratings help collaborative filtering, but they do nothing for a user
who has rated *nothing* — cold start is a structural gap, not a volume problem — and they cannot fix a
mismatch between optimizing RMSE and optimizing what users actually want.

**"Is offline RMSE the final word?"** No. Offline metrics are how you *screen* ideas cheaply; the real
test is an **online A/B test** on live users, because recommendations change the very behavior you
measure. (Online evaluation is beyond this course; we name it so you know the offline number is a
start, not the verdict.)

## Ethics

Demographic filtering groups people by age, gender, or region — convenient, but it can encode and
amplify bias, and "people like you" can quietly become "people boxed in like you." Content-based
over-specialization is how **filter bubbles** form. Optimizing a single offline number (watch time,
clicks) is how engagement-at-any-cost systems arise. **Unit VIII** takes these up directly.

## Key Takeaways

- **Content-based** uses item features (genres): a centered-rating-weighted profile, scored by cosine.
  It handles new items (Ana's *Die Hard*), but genres are coarse — scores tie, and a quality signal
  breaks the tie — and it over-specializes.
- **Demographic** (user attributes) and **knowledge-based** (stated rules) need no rating history from
  the target user, so they can run where collaborative filtering cannot. Running is not predicting
  well: on MovieLens, cohort averages tie with plain item means.
- **Hybrid** systems (switching or weighted) combine families; a hybrid covers a gap only if one of its
  parts does.
- **Evaluate** with a held-out split: **RMSE** (punishes big misses) and **MAE** (average miss). The
  ladder — global mean, item mean, baseline, item-item CF, matrix factorization — is read by its
  steps: the baseline does most of the work, CF ties it, the latent factors add the last small step.
- **RMSE/MAE measure rating prediction; ranking quality (precision@k) is a related but different goal.**

## Cheat-sheet

| Task | Idea |
|---|---|
| Content profile | sum of the rated items' feature vectors, each weighted by the user's centered rating |
| Content score | cosine(profile, item-feature vector); ties on coarse features, break them with a stated quality signal |
| Demographic pick | top-rated items within a user cohort (`groupby` attributes); can run for a new user |
| Knowledge-based pick | filter by stated constraints (genre, year); a min-rating filter is borrowed from ratings |
| Hybrid | switch between families, or blend their (min-max scaled) scores |
| Evaluate | `train_test_split`, clip to 1-5, then RMSE $\sqrt{\text{mean}((\hat r - r)^2)}$ and MAE |
| Baseline rung | $\hat r_{ui} = \mu + b_u + b_i$ (L22); a model must beat it to earn its place (item-item CF only ties it here) |

## Where to Go Deeper

- **Survey:** [Microsoft Recommenders (GitHub)](https://github.com/recommenders-team/recommenders) — production-grade examples of content, collaborative, and hybrid recommenders with evaluation.
- **Evaluation:** [scikit-learn — Model evaluation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html) — RMSE/MAE and the broader metric landscape (ranking metrics included).
- **Baselines:** Y. Koren (2010). *Factor in the Neighbors: Scalable and Accurate Collaborative Filtering.* ACM TKDD — why the user and item biases come first, and how neighborhood models are built on top of them.
- **Hybrids:** R. Burke (2002). *Hybrid Recommender Systems: Survey and Experiments.* User Modeling and User-Adapted Interaction — the classic taxonomy of switching/weighted/cascade hybrids.
